newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador measures seen falling short of fiscal aims.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador measures seen falling short of fiscal aims.

text.p: A range of measures launched Friday night by Ecuadoran caretaker President Fabian Alarcon will fall short of his goverment's goals to trim the fiscal gap and foster economic growth, analysts said Saturday.

"The economic program will not reach its proposed objectives to cut the fiscal deficit," economic analyst Walter Spurrier told Reuters. "I don't think the economy will grow by the amount stated by the President."
Alarcon was named President in February by Congress to replace Abdala Bucaram who was dismissed for "mental incapacity."

He has launched a battery of measures to cut the 1997 fiscal gap from 6.6 percent of GDP to 2.5 percent, and has said that could be attained by a 10 percent or $400 million budget cut and $150 million in additional tax collection.

But Luis Jacome, director of an economic research think-tank, said, "The program involves moderate adjustments that don't make sense given the current economic imbalances, and it jeopardizes the fiscal management of 1998."
At most, Jacome said, the measures could trim the fiscal gap to three or four percent.
Spurrier said, "Alarcon has a special mandate ... he doesn't have much room to maneuver, and he is doing what's possible to put the economy in order, but what's possible is not enough.
"The most difficult issue will be to win over the IMF to his economic program, which would limit the possibilities of renegotiating the country's debt with the Paris Club."
The government has said it plans to renegotiate its $2 billion debt to the Paris Club.

Rising inflation and the elimination by Bucaram of monthly fuel prices hikes has deprived the government of a huge amount of income, analysts said. Inflation was 26 percent in 1996 and experts see it accelerating to 30 percent this year.
The analysts said that if the government tries to cut the fiscal gap by issuing domestic debt, interest rates would jump, creating greater unemployment.
A better alternative might be to take on external debt, issuing the $300 million Eurobonds whose launch was interrupted by the political turmoil that led to Bucaram's dismissal, they said.
Economists also doubt the economy will grow by 3.5 percent this year and four percent next year as Alarcon expects.
